statement: A drawer holds $4$ different pairs of gloves, $8$ gloves in all. Each pair has one left glove and one right glove. Ellie takes out $2$ gloves at random. What is the probability that she gets one left glove and one right glove that do not belong to the same pair?

choices.misconception: I found the probability of a left and a right glove from the same pair, 4 out of 28, instead of from different pairs.
I treated the second draw as if the first glove went back in the drawer, so I got 2 x (4/8) x (3/8) = 3/8.
I thought each glove is a left or a right like a coin flip, so getting one of each happens half the time.
I counted every left and right combination, 4 x 4 = 16 out of 28, but forgot to remove the 4 matching pairs.

hints: Count the ways to choose $2$ of the $8$ gloves, and count the good choices.
There are $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ ways to choose the gloves. A left and a right can be chosen in $4 \times 4$ ways.
Of the $16$ left and right combinations, $4$ are matching pairs and must be removed.

solutions.reliable: There are $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ equally likely ways to choose $2$ gloves. Choosing one left glove and one right glove can be done in $4 \times 4 = 16$ ways, and exactly $4$ of these are matching pairs. So $16 - 4 = 12$ choices are good, and the probability is $\frac{12}{28} = \frac{3}{7}$.
solutions.elegant: Whatever Ellie's first glove is, $7$ gloves remain, and exactly $3$ of them are of the opposite hand and from a different pair. So the probability is $\frac{3}{7}$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
